scenes.text: So, why does practice that looks worse work better? Two groups learn three tennis strokes over six sessions, with the same number of hits. Group A does thirty forehands, then thirty backhands, then thirty volleys. Group B does the same ninety, shuffled, never knowing which stroke comes next. By session six, group A looks far better. Two weeks later, both groups are tested, and group B wins comfortably. What was group B doing on every hit that group A wasn't?

Group A did blocked practice: one skill repeated many times before the next. Group B did random practice: several skills mixed in an unpredictable order. In blocked practice, each hit is a small tweak of the last, so it looks smooth. In random practice, the other strokes push the plan out of mind, so on every hit she rebuilds it from scratch. That rebuilding is hard work, makes each hit worse, and is exactly what a match demands. So we need two words. Performance is how well you do it right now. Learning is a lasting change, and you only see it later, in a retention test after a delay. A coach at training sees performance, and hopes for learning. Here they moved in opposite directions. One catch: a beginner has no plan to rebuild yet. So block to acquire, then shuffle to retain.

Two more choices have clear rules. Massed practice has little rest. Distributed practice has real rest between attempts or sessions. A beginner usually needs distributed practice, because the movement uses all her attention, and a tired beginner practises errors. Practice doesn't make perfect, it makes permanent. Massed practice suits short, easy skills and experienced learners. Whole practice does the full skill, and part practice splits it. The scale from last time decides. A continuous skill is mostly taught as a whole, with drills like kick and pull as practice parts. A serial skill can be split, then joined two parts at a time, then done whole.

The syllabus also names performance elements, the parts of an open skill that aren't the movement. Decision-making is choosing the right response, under time pressure, with incomplete information. A drill with one right answer can't train it. Small-sided games and drills with two real options can. A coach calling out a shuffled order isn't a decision, either. The player has to choose from what she reads. Strategy is the plan made before a contest, like pressing high. Tactics are changes made during it, like whether to keep pressing when you're two goals down. Strategy is planned by studying the opposition, then rehearsed in training. Tactics grow from game situations and questions. Before, or during: that's the difference.

The syllabus names six types of feedback, but they're really three questions, and every comment answers all three. Where did it come from? Task-intrinsic feedback comes from doing the skill: what you feel, see and hear. Augmented feedback is added from outside, by a coach, a video or a timing gate. When did it arrive? Concurrent feedback comes during the movement, and delayed feedback after it. Concurrent feedback only helps when the movement is slow enough to act on, like a long swim, not a half-second shot. And what is it about? Knowledge of results is the outcome: it went wide. Knowledge of performance is the movement that caused it: your shoulders opened early. A player who's just missed already knows the result. What she needs is the reason.

And here's the same twist again. Frequent, instant, detailed feedback makes a session look better, and learning worse. The learner stops attending to her own feel, because a better source is always there. Then in a match, her own feel is all she has, and she's never learnt to read it. So fade it: less often, a little later, and ask, how did that feel, before you tell her.

Put it together by stage. A cognitive learner gets distributed, blocked practice, parts for a complex skill, and immediate feedback on one point. An associative learner moves toward random practice, with feedback delayed and asked for first. An autonomous performer practises whole, random and game-like, and mostly reads their own feedback. Every row runs one way, from outside to inside. The coach's job is to hand it over.
Two things to remember. Block to acquire, shuffle to retain. And feedback moves from outside to inside: ask before you tell.

Two exam questions. First. After training, a long jumper's coach shows her a video of her take-off that evening, and says her last stride was too long. Classify this feedback on all three questions. Pause here to answer.

It's augmented, because it comes from the coach and the video. It's delayed, because it arrives hours after the jump. And it's knowledge of performance, because it's about her stride, not her distance. The classic mistake is calling a video knowledge of results just because it shows the jump.

Second. A beginner in her first month of golf gets no comments during sessions. At the end of each week, her coach tells her only how many putts she made. Explain why this feedback suits her poorly, and what the coach should do instead. Pause here to answer.

She's a cognitive learner, so she can't yet detect her own errors. A weekly putt count is delayed knowledge of results, and it says nothing about what to change. She needs prompt augmented feedback on one point of the movement, knowledge of performance, then less of it as she becomes associative. The classic mistake is thinking less feedback is always better.

So, for any learner, choose practice and feedback by their stage, and judge it by retention, not by how the session looked. But that blocked and random result is a big claim, and everyone has an opinion about coaching. Where did it come from? How do you check what the evidence says?
